intro: Roosendaal's registered trees cluster around three public spots: De Kring square, where a rare Oriental plane and a horse chestnut both grow within sight of each other; Emile van Loonpark, where a chestnut stands behind the pond that its own registered lime, declared dead back in 1998, no longer overlooks; and Burgerhoutsestraat, where a catalpa and a London plane frame the same building from opposite sides. A beech behind a restaurant and a fast-growing poplar on a car park round out the list.
meta_description: Seven registered trees in Roosendaal: a rare Oriental plane at De Kring, a chestnut by the Van Loonpark pond, and a catalpa on Burgerhoutsestraat.
question_meta: Roosendaal's oldest tree is a horse chestnut at De Kring, banded to around 1840 and roughly 190 years old. Its story and seven more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Roosendaal is the Horse Chestnut of De Kring, which the national tree register bands to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old. It stands on De Kring square beside a rare Oriental plane the register also lists.
question_context: Ages here come from the Landelijk Register Monumentale Bomen, which records a planting decade rather than a year, so every figure on this page is a band. The register is the single source throughout, so every entry ships flagged rather than confirmed. Three spots carry two trees each: De Kring square holds the Oriental plane and the horse chestnut, Burgerhoutsestraat holds a catalpa and a London plane at opposite corners of the same building, and Emile van Loonpark holds a horse chestnut behind the pond. The park's own lime, which the register originally listed alongside that chestnut, was declared dead back in 1998 and does not appear on this page, since a tree known to be gone never ships as a collectible entry here. A beech behind Restaurant Vrouwenhof and a fast-growing Canadian poplar on the Bloemenmarkt car park round out the list. Where a pin is marked approximate, we know the site and not the exact trunk.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Roosendaal?
faq.a: The Horse Chestnut of De Kring, banded by the national tree register to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old. It stands on De Kring square beside a rare Oriental plane.

faq.q: What happened to the lime in Emile van Loonpark?
faq.a: The national register records it as declared dead in 1998. It does not appear on this list: a tree known to be gone is never published as a collectible entry here, however long it stood. The park's horse chestnut, behind the pond, is still there.

faq.q: Why does an Oriental plane at De Kring stand out?
faq.a: Most planes planted on Dutch squares are London planes, a hybrid bred from the Oriental species and an American one. This is the wilder-growing parent itself, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, planted here around 1850.

faq.q: Are these trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes. Every tree on this list stands on a public square, park or car park, free to see at any time.

trees.name: The Oriental Plane of De Kring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 180 years, from a registered planting date around 1850
trees.story:
This Oriental plane stands by De Kring, a public square in Roosendaal, banded by the national register to a planting around 1850, roughly 180 years old. It shares the square with a horse chestnut the register also lists, the two trees framing the same small public space from different corners.

Oriental plane is the older, wilder-growing parent of the hybrid London plane that lines so many European streets, native to southeast Europe and western Asia, and it is planted less often in the Netherlands than its more tolerant offspring. Left to grow on an open square rather than pruned to a street profile, an Oriental plane develops the same flaking, camouflage-patterned bark as its hybrid relative but with a more irregular, spreading crown, often leaning and forking low rather than rising in a single clean trunk.

The register records the species and the decade but nothing of who planted it or why, which is typical for a tree whose interest is simply having survived on the same square for nearly two centuries while whatever stood around it changed. If you know more of De Kring's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of De Kring
trees.age_estimate: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840

location.address: Roosendaal, Kerkstraat 1, bij De Kring Roosendaal

trees.story:
This horse chestnut shares De Kring square with the Oriental plane the register also lists nearby, banded to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old and a decade older than its neighbour. Two trees of very different origins, one from the eastern Mediterranean and one from the mountains of the Balkans, ended up planted within a stone's throw of each other on an ordinary Dutch town square, which is itself a small piece of nineteenth century planting fashion: whatever looked handsome and grew reliably got planted, regardless of where it came from.

At close to two centuries a horse chestnut has usually developed the full domed crown and heavy lower limbs the species is known for, wide enough that a tree this age can shade most of a small square by itself. Every May it produces the upright white candle-shaped flower spikes chestnuts are grown for everywhere, and by autumn the ground beneath is scattered with the spiny green cases and glossy conkers that generations of Dutch children have collected from trees exactly like this one.

The register gives no history beyond species and decade. If you know more, tell us.

best_time.label: May, when the white candle-shaped flower spikes cover the crown

trees.name: The Catalpa of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 130 years, from a registered planting date around 1900
trees.story:
This catalpa stands southwest of a building on Burgerhoutsestraat, banded by the national register to a planting around 1900, roughly 130 years old. A London plane the register also lists grows at the front of the same building, so the property carries two registered trees framing it from different sides, one native to the eastern United States and one a hybrid bred in seventeenth century Europe.

Southern catalpa is grown for its broad, heart-shaped leaves and, through midsummer, loose clusters of white flowers marked with purple and yellow spots inside each throat, followed by long, bean-like seed pods that can hang on the bare branches well into winter, giving the species its other common name, Indian bean tree, despite having no connection to India.

A catalpa at 130 years is well into a mature specimen's proportions, wide-crowned and often leaning or multi-stemmed if it was ever cut back hard when young. The register records nothing of who planted it or why, only the species and the decade. If you know more about this tree or the building it stands beside, tell us.

best_time.label: July, when the orchid-like flowers open in loose clusters across the crown

trees.name: The Beech of Vrouwenhof
trees.age_estimate: roughly 190 years, from a registered planting date around 1840
trees.story:
This beech stands behind Restaurant Vrouwenhof, banded by the national register to a planting around 1840, roughly 190 years old. Left alone behind a building rather than beside a road, a beech this age has usually had the easiest kind of life the species can have: no pruning against traffic, no root compaction from foot or vehicle traffic, room enough to build the wide, low, dome-shaped crown that beeches produce when nothing crowds them.

A beech's bark stays smooth and grey its entire life, never cracking into plates the way an oak's does, which is part of why old beeches are the trees most often carved with initials that never grow over. At nearly two centuries this one has likely accumulated its share, along with the deep leaf litter underneath that beech woodland is known for, since almost nothing grows in the permanent shade a mature beech casts.

The register describes nothing of the tree's own history beyond species and decade, which is typical for a tree valued for standing rather than for any single event attached to it. If you know more, tell us.

trees.name: The Poplar of the Bloemenmarkt
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870
trees.story:
This Canadian poplar grows on a car park at the Bloemenmarkt, Roosendaal's flower market square, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. Canadian poplar is itself a hybrid, crossed from American and European black poplars sometime in the eighteenth century and planted across Europe ever since for how fast it grows: a young tree can add a metre or more of height a year, reaching a size in a few decades that other species take a century to match.

That speed comes at a cost in longevity and structural soundness, so a Canadian poplar surviving to 160 years, on a car park rather than in a sheltered park setting, is a genuinely long run for the species. Poplars of this age often carry visible deadwood and cavities, part of what makes a veteran specimen valuable as habitat even as it becomes more likely to lose limbs in storms.

The register records nothing about this tree beyond its species and decade. Growing up on a car park rather than a green space is an unusual setting for the list; if you know how it came to be there, tell us.

trees.name: The Horse Chestnut of the Pond
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Roosendaal, Emile van Loonpark, achter vijver

trees.story:
This horse chestnut stands behind the pond in Emile van Loonpark, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old. The park's own lime, registered elsewhere on this list's original candidates, was declared dead as far back as 1998, which makes this chestnut the park's surviving veteran rather than one of a matched pair.

A horse chestnut planted beside water has usually had reliable growing conditions its whole life, and at 160 years this one should show the full domed crown and heavy branch structure the species develops when left largely alone. Every May it produces the upright white flower spikes chestnuts are planted for across Europe, and reflected in the pond behind it, the display reads differently than a chestnut standing on hard pavement elsewhere in this list.

The register gives no further history for this tree, only species and decade. Emile van Loonpark is public and open daily, and this chestnut is the reason to walk to the far side of the pond rather than stopping at the park's edge. If you know more about it, tell us.

best_time.label: May, when the white flower spikes cover the crown and reflect in the pond

trees.name: The Plane of Burgerhoutsestraat
trees.age_estimate: roughly 160 years, from a registered planting date around 1870

location.address: Roosendaal, Burgerhoutsestraat 12, aan de voorzijde van het gebouw

trees.story:
This London plane stands at the front of the same Burgerhoutsestraat building whose southwest corner holds a registered catalpa, banded by the national register to a planting around 1870, roughly 160 years old and a generation younger than its catalpa neighbour on the other side of the same property.

London plane is the hybrid that resulted from crossing an American and an Oriental species in seventeenth century Europe, and it turned out to tolerate compacted soil, air pollution and hard pruning better than almost any other large tree available, which is why it became the default choice for European streets and squares from the eighteenth century onward. Its bark flakes away in patches rather than splitting, leaving a mottled grey, green and cream pattern across the trunk that keeps changing as old plates drop and new bark shows through underneath.

At the front of a building rather than tucked behind it, this plane has likely had more pruning against passing traffic than its catalpa neighbour, which a plane tolerates without much complaint. The register records only species and decade. If you know the building's own history, tell us.

trees.name: The Dutch Lime of Emile van Loonpark
trees.age_estimate: roughly 225 to 275 years, from a registered planting band of 1750-1800
trees.transport: Roosendaal railway station, about 5 min walk
trees.notes: LRMB register nr 1680922 ('Hollandse linde'), owner category gemeente, setting park, listed as publicly visitable. The register's own history notes for this location mention a much earlier tree at the same spot declared dead in 1998; that note describes the PLACE's older history, not this currently registered tree, and is not carried into the story to avoid a bridge claim. Single source; a second is wanted.
trees.story:
Roosendaal's Dutch lime in Emile van Loonpark carries a planting band rather than a single year: the Netherlands' national register of monumental trees puts it somewhere between 1750 and 1800. That makes it older than the park around it, which the mayor of the same name only began laying out in 1883, roughly a century after this lime was already growing on the site.

The register lists it as municipal property standing on open parkland, one of the smaller number of Roosendaal's trees old enough to carry the monumental designation at all. Its current girth and condition are not recorded in what we could find so far.

A common lime this old has usually been pollarded, coppiced or propped at some point, since the species tends to hollow at the base long before it dies outright. Whether this one carries that history is worth a look on the ground. It rests on one source for now, the register itself: if you have stood under it, tell us what you saw.
